name: Tatana
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Dillon, John Albert (1994) A Grammatical Description of Tatana' (Univ. of Texas at Arlington thesis; named on Wikipedia 'Tatana language'); SIL search returned 403

new_statements.quote: There are twenty-one segmental phonemes in Tatana': seventeen consonants /p t k ʔ b d g s dʒ m n ɲ ŋ l r w y/ and four vowels /i u o a/. Stress is noncontrastive.
new_statements.citation: Pekkanen, Inka. 1993. Tatana' phonemics. In Michael E. Boutin & Inka Pekkanen (eds.), Phonological descriptions of Sabah languages: Studies from ten languages (Sabah Museum Monograph 4). Kota Kinabalu: Sabah Museum. p. 15.
new_statements.locator: Section 2 'Phonemes', p. 15 (first sentence of the section); supporting phonetic transcriptions in sec. 2.1.1 'Consonants', pp. 16-18
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not phonemic (non-contrastive). The source gives no explicit placement rule in the scanned pages, but every phonetic form it transcribes carries the stress mark on the penultimate syllable, in disyllables (['anak] 'child', ['manuk] 'chicken', ['kanaʔ] 'fish', ['paya] 'tired') and trisyllables alike ([si'siog] 'bird', [mə'ɲuluŋ] 'will slip on'); /maraat/ 'bad' is transcribed [ma'ra:t] with stress on the (coalesced) long vowel. So the provisional reading is predictable penultimate stress; the explicit statement is only that stress is non-contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the scanned pages.
new_statements.exceptions: None in the phonemics excerpt. Pekkanen & Chan 1989 (Learn to speak Tatana', p. 23) note an utterance-level pattern: a one-word affirmative answer repeating the verb has its last syllable stressed and slightly lengthened with falling intonation — intonational, not lexical.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (citation forms in a phoneme inventory, with phonetic transcriptions of isolated words). Data from Kinontungan and Kulung-Kulung villages, Kuala Penyu, collected May 1980-April 1981 (p. 15, fn. 1).
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Tatana' of Kinontungan and Kulung-Kulung villages, Kuala Penyu District, Sabah (the language has no recognised dialect divisions per Dunn 1984, p. 251); same variety as tata1257 / ISO txx. Note that Pekkanen 1993 gives four vowels /i u o a/ whereas Dillon 1994 (via Wikipedia/PHOIBLE) gives five (/i u a ə ɔ/) — an analytic difference, not a different variety.
